text: Every AllReduce from the last lesson is, underneath, a networking event — gradients have to physically move between GPUs, on every step, for the whole training run. This lesson is about the interconnects that move that traffic, and why how they're wired matters as much as how fast they are.

Inside a single server, GPUs still need to talk to each other constantly, and the standard PCIe bus — topping out around sixty-four gigabytes per second — isn't close to enough. NVLink is NVIDIA's answer: a direct GPU-to-GPU link that bypasses PCIe and the CPU entirely, and combined with NVSwitch, lets every GPU in a server reach every other GPU at hundreds of gigabytes per second, up toward a terabyte per second. That's why tensor parallelism, which needs extremely fast per-layer communication, normally stays confined to GPUs inside one NVLink-connected machine.

Once a job spans more than one server, traffic has to cross a real network, and ordinary Ethernet with a standard TCP stack adds too much latency and CPU overhead. Training clusters use InfiniBand instead, paired with RDMA — specifically GPUDirect RDMA, which lets one machine's GPU write straight into another machine's GPU memory, skipping both CPUs and main memory entirely. That two-tier structure, NVLink inside the box and InfiniBand between boxes, is exactly why pipeline parallelism, which tolerates coarser communication, is what usually stretches across that slower link.

Fast links alone aren't enough if they're wired together badly. Bisection bandwidth asks: if you split the cluster in half, how much bandwidth actually exists between the two halves? A topology with low bisection bandwidth bottlenecks exactly where AllReduce needs to move the most data. Fat-tree and rail-optimized designs exist specifically to keep that number high as a cluster scales — a cluster can have the best NICs money can buy and still underperform if the switching fabric between them is oversubscribed.

Here's the counterintuitive part: as a job adds more GPUs, each one's share of compute per step shrinks, but AllReduce still has to move every gradient across the fabric on every single step. Past a certain scale, synchronization time can exceed compute time, and faster GPUs simply stop helping until the network problem gets solved. That's why NCCL implements AllReduce as a ring or tree pattern rather than naive all-to-all — built specifically to use the topology efficiently. Next lesson turns to a different kind of risk entirely: what happens when, days into a training run, a node just fails.
